blocks.text: Multiple Linear Regression extended linear regression to many features at once, but every one of those features still genuinely combined into a straight, flat hyperplane. Polynomial regression addresses the real, remaining limitation both regression topics so far have shared, capturing genuinely curved relationships, while staying entirely within the exact same linear regression machinery covered in both previous topics.

This topic covers how polynomial regression directly reuses the Polynomial Features technique first covered back in Feature Engineering, a genuinely important, often misunderstood conceptual point, why this technique still counts as linear regression despite producing a visibly curved fit, the real degree and overfitting tradeoff first covered in that earlier topic, now applied directly to an actual fitted model, and the standard pipeline used to combine both steps together.
1. Directly Reusing Polynomial Features

blocks.alt: Polynomial features feed directly into linear regression

blocks.text: Polynomial regression genuinely takes an original feature, x, and adds x squared, and optionally x cubed and beyond, as brand new columns, exactly the technique covered in full back in Polynomial Features. Those expanded columns are then genuinely fed into an ordinary linear regression, exactly the same fitting process covered in the two previous topics, with no change to the underlying algorithm at all.

This is genuinely worth being direct about, polynomial regression is not a new, separate algorithm, it is linear regression applied to a genuinely cleverly expanded set of features, precisely the technique this course already built in the Feature Engineering module, now finally put to its real, intended use in an actual fitted model.
2. A Genuinely Important, Often Misunderstood Point

blocks.alt: A curved relationship in X is still linear in the coefficients

blocks.text: It is genuinely, easily assumed that a curved fit must come from some fundamentally different, nonlinear algorithm. The real, actual truth is that linear regression genuinely means linear in the coefficients, the weights being learned, not linear in the original feature x itself. Once x squared exists as its own genuine column, the model is still genuinely just adding up weighted columns, exactly the same operation as every previous regression topic, it simply has a curved column, x squared, among its inputs.

This distinction matters directly for understanding this entire course regression module structure, polynomial regression genuinely belongs here, alongside the straight line techniques, precisely because the fitting method itself never actually changes.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Polynomial regression is genuinely still linear regression, mathematically, linear in the coefficients being learned, not in the original feature values. The curve comes entirely from the expanded features, not from a different fitting algorithm.

blocks.text: 3. A Worked Example

blocks.alt: Curved data fit with a degree 2 polynomial produces a good fit

blocks.text: Chaining PolynomialFeatures and LinearRegression together with scikit-learn Pipeline shows this entire technique applied directly, on a genuinely curved, accelerating relationship.

code.content:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
import numpy as np

speed = np.array([[20], [40], [60], [80], [100]])
braking_distance = np.array([6, 20, 42, 74, 112])

model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree=2), LinearRegression())
model.fit(speed, braking_distance)

print("Predicted braking distance at 70:", model.predict([[70]])[0])

blocks.text: The pipeline genuinely handles both steps internally, expanding speed into speed and speed squared, then fitting ordinary linear regression on that expanded pair, correctly capturing the genuine accelerating, curved relationship between speed and braking distance first introduced back in Polynomial Features.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Always use make_pipeline to bundle PolynomialFeatures with LinearRegression rather than applying them as two separate, manual steps. This genuinely keeps the exact same expansion applied consistently to new, future data.

blocks.text: 4. Capturing a Genuinely Real, Curved Relationship

blocks.alt: A straight line misses the curve while a polynomial curve fits it

blocks.text: Braking distance versus speed, the exact real example first covered in Polynomial Features, genuinely does not grow at a steady, constant rate, it grows genuinely faster as speed increases, a real, accelerating, curved relationship that plain linear or multiple regression would consistently underestimate at high speeds and overestimate at low speeds.

Polynomial regression genuinely fits this real curve directly, precisely because the squared speed term is now available as its own genuine feature for the model to assign a weight to, capturing the accelerating real pattern that a bare, unexpanded speed feature alone could never represent.
5. The Same Degree and Overfitting Tradeoff

blocks.alt: A low degree underfits while a high degree overfits

blocks.text: Choosing a polynomial degree here carries genuinely the exact same tradeoff covered back in Polynomial Features, a genuinely low degree produces a smooth, sensible curve that captures the real underlying pattern, while a genuinely high degree can produce a wild, wiggly curve that fits the specific training data noise rather than any real, generalizable pattern.

This is worth restating directly in this fitted model context, choosing a polynomial degree is genuinely not just a feature engineering decision anymore, it is directly, simultaneously a model complexity decision, with the exact same real overfitting risk that degree choice carried in the earlier, purely feature focused topic.

blocks.text: 6. The Model Complexity Spectrum

blocks.alt: The model complexity spectrum runs from simple to complex

blocks.text: Degree 1 genuinely reduces directly back to plain linear regression, no curve at all. Degree 2 genuinely introduces one real bend, degree 3 genuinely allows up to two, and every additional degree genuinely adds more flexibility, and more real risk of overfitting, continuing the exact spectrum first laid out back in Power Transformation ladder of powers.

This spectrum is worth holding onto directly when choosing a degree for a real, specific problem, start genuinely low, and only increase it when there is real, concrete evidence, checked against a genuine validation set, that the underlying relationship actually needs more flexibility than a lower degree provides.
7. The Standard Pipeline Approach

blocks.alt: A raw feature goes through a polynomial features step, then a linear model step

blocks.text: Chaining PolynomialFeatures and LinearRegression together into a single scikit-learn Pipeline, exactly as shown in the worked example above, keeps both steps genuinely bundled as one coherent unit, fitting the expansion and the regression together, and applying that exact same fitted expansion consistently to any new, future data.

This is genuinely the standard, practical way this technique gets applied in real projects, rather than manually expanding features and fitting a separate model by hand, a pipeline keeps the entire process genuinely reproducible and consistent between training and later prediction.

blocks.text: 8. Polynomial Regression Versus What Comes Next

Linear, Multiple Linear, and Polynomial Regression together cover the genuine core family built directly on ordinary least squares, one feature, many features, and now curved relationships, all fit with the exact same underlying fitting method. Every one of these three topics, though, shares a real, genuine risk, especially as more features or a higher polynomial degree get involved, overfitting to the specific training data.

The next topic, Ridge Regression, addresses that exact real risk directly, introducing regularization, a genuine, direct way to control model complexity and reduce overfitting, extending the exact same linear regression framework this entire module opened with.

items: Polynomial regression genuinely reuses the Polynomial Features technique, then fits ordinary linear regression on the expansion.
It genuinely remains linear regression mathematically, linear in the coefficients, not linear in the original feature.
It genuinely captures real, curved relationships like braking distance versus speed that straight line regression cannot.
Choosing a polynomial degree genuinely carries the same real overfitting risk covered back in Polynomial Features.
Higher degrees genuinely add more flexibility and genuinely more overfitting risk, continuing that same spectrum.
The next topic, Ridge Regression, genuinely introduces regularization to directly control that real overfitting risk.
